title: Wages held back (James 5:1–6)
hook: the wages you withheld cry out

segments.voice: Yesterday, if the Lord wills, and your line was a little while. Which good thing did you stop saving for someday? Day six hundred seventy-eight.

A day laborer in the ancient world lived on one day's pay. In the morning he went to the marketplace and waited to be hired. In the evening he was paid, and that money bought the family's bread for the next day. No savings account. No paycheck next Friday. If the landowner said, come back next week, the children didn't eat. That's the world behind today's passage. And James, who has been gentle and practical for four chapters, suddenly raises his voice. This is the sharpest paragraph in his letter.

In the King James Bible: "Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you." It sounds like the old prophets, Amos or Isaiah, thundering against injustice. Then pictures of wealth rotting where it's stored: "Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten." The gold and silver, he says, have rusted, and the rust will be a witness against you. Hoarded things decay. Then the heart of it: "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth." The wages themselves cry out. Money that should have been in a worker's hand has a voice. And it reaches God. The law of Moses was clear on this. Deuteronomy says to pay a poor laborer his wage on the same day, before the sun goes down, because he is poor and his heart is set on it, so that he doesn't cry to the Lord against you. James is drawing on that old command. And notice the title he uses for God. Lord of sabaoth. It isn't sabbath. It's a Hebrew word meaning armies, or hosts. The Lord of hosts. The commander of heaven's armies is listening to the cry of a farmhand who wasn't paid. Christians have heard this passage in every age where workers were cheated, from fields to factories. Many churches have taught from it that a fair wage, paid on time, isn't charity. It's justice.
screen: then, large: `KEPT BACK BY FRAUD, CRIETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay someone promptly. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people whose work you depend on that you rarely see. The person who picks your fruit. Who cleans the office at night. Who delivers the packages. Who sews the clothes you're wearing. Picture one of them. Then think closer to home: do you owe anyone right now? An invoice, a babysitter, a friend who covered lunch, a bill you've let slide. Name it. Decide when you'll pay. If you pray, you can pray for workers who are waiting on wages. The bell holds the time.
Wages held back. Pay kept from workers by fraud, which, James says, cries out to the Lord of hosts.
Your line: the wages cry out. Today, pay one thing you owe, a bill, a loan, a babysitter, sooner than you have to. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Many churches draw on James 5 and Deuteronomy 24 in their teaching on fair wages and workers' rights, and some congregations make a point of paying their own staff and contractors promptly and fairly.
